item.title: Distance from the climatic niche optimum explains climate‐change‐driven dynamics in Mediterranean shrublands
item.description:

Understanding vegetation responses to climatic variability is essential for anticipating future trajectories and informing management and conservation. Climatic niche metrics can improve climatic impact assessments by accounting for species‐specific climatic requirements. We analysed vegetation responses to gradual changes in climatic conditions in the monte blanco shrubland of Doñana National Park (SW Spain), one of Europe's most biodiverse protected areas. Specifically, we assessed vegetation dynamics over a 15‐year period (2007–2022) following a drought‐induced canopy loss event. We used species' climatic niche centroids as a proxy for their climatic optima and quantified their distance to observed climatic conditions as an indicator of climatic disequilibrium. item.title: Partitioning the variance of species–area relation into sampling‐ versus scale‐dependent components
item.description:
相关度 69.9 · 关键词匹配：species richness、uncertainty、spatial scale

The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample. We establish this decomposition mathematically and evaluate its behavior through numerical simulations. On this basis, empirical SAR observations can be classified as falling within the conditional confidence interval (CI), within the gap between the conditional and unconditional CIs, or outside the unconditional CI. item.description:

Invasive tree pests and pathogens are increasingly threatening forests worldwide. Understanding how a warming climate and changing precipitation patterns will affect the future distribution ranges of these pathogenic species requires systematic analysis across a variety of host trees and pathogenic species. We analysed 31 major tree pests and pathogens that have caused widespread and extensive damage globally, predicting their current and future distribution under various climate change scenarios using species distribution modelling. Our results showed that tree pests and pathogens will consistently shift northward, threatening northern temperate and boreal forests between the years 2041 and 2080. Aims Data from participatory science projects are widely used to understand species distributions. However, participatory science data often contain biases that can obscure real patterns. We address two sources of sampling bias: location uncertainty of individual records and spatially heterogeneous sampling effort. We test several strategies using data from iNaturalist, a large repository of participatory science data. Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we assessed whether squamate reptiles inside PAs experience lower heat exposure than conspecifics in unprotected, human‐modified landscapes, and how this buffering effect varies across latitudes, biomes, and evolutionary lineages. Using biophysical modelling of operative temperatures across 248 species, we show that PAs consistently reduced both annual hours above critical thermal maximum (CT max ) and the frequency of critical days under current and future climatic scenarios (+2°C and + 4°C). item.description:
相关度 69.7 · 关键词匹配：range shift、climate change、latitudinal gradient

Climate change is expected to drive substantial shifts in species distributions, yet ecological responses are often delayed under disequilibrium dynamics, limiting the effectiveness of range‐based indicators for detecting ongoing change. Compositional approaches have been proposed as an alternative; however, conventional comparisons based on gradient shape or pointwise differences may fail to detect change when the overall gradient structure is conserved, because small and spatially heterogeneous differences cancel out across the gradient. Here, we address this limitation by presenting a direction‐sensitive analytical framework that integrates signed differences along environmental gradients. item.description:

Variable importance derived from species distribution modelling (SDM) is widely used to identify key environmental drivers of species distributions. However, the reliability of these inferences has rarely been systematically evaluated, particularly with respect to their sensitivity to individual occurrences. Here, we used virtual species and developed a sample perturbations diagnostic framework, in which each occurrence was systematically removed (leave‐one‐out) to assess how small changes in the input data affect variable importance inference. Using this framework, we evaluated and compared ten SDM algorithms across multiple scenarios. We constructed a set of evaluation metrics to quantify both the accuracy of driver identification and the stability of permutation importance estimates, defined as their variability under sample perturbations. item.description:
相关度 73.4 · 关键词匹配：climate change、biogeography、species richness

The metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) conceptualizes that temperature is the primary driver of species richness, a pattern well supported in terrestrial taxa but less certain for freshwater organisms. Limited global‐scale evidence and frequent violations of MTE's assumptions, particularly regarding the stationarity of body size and abundance, further undermine its applicability. In freshwater systems, body size and abundance are tightly linked to dispersal and range size, which differ markedly between running‐water (lotic) and standing‐water (lentic) species, as proposed by the Habitat‐Stability–Dispersal Hypothesis (HSDH). Adaptations to habitat stability may therefore generate distinct biogeographical patterns of traits and modify richness–temperature relationships predicted by MTE. Understanding how anthropogenic pressures and environmental gradients shape coastal fish communities is a central question in biogeography and marine conservation. Yet, the set of species expected to occur at a site given ecological conditions but being absent – the so‐called dark diversity – has received far less attention than observed species, even if they hold key information about local extirpations and conservation effectiveness. Quantifying dark diversity in the sea is particularly challenging because many species are rare, cryptobenthic or mobile, while sampling effort is rarely standardized. Here we combined 930 environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected at 401 sites along 2000 km of the French Mediterranean coast with fine‐scale mapping of habitats, anthropogenic pressures and protection levels. Systematic conservation planning provides a science‐based framework for defining conservation goals and supporting transparent spatial decision‐making under limited resources. Within this framework, spatial conservation prioritisation tools are widely used to identify areas of high biodiversity value by integrating information on species distributions, connectivity, costs, and other factors into spatially explicit recommendations. ‘Zonation' is one of the leading software tools in this field, producing hierarchical priority rankings of landscapes based on conservation value. However, its standard workflow typically relies on manual steps for data preparation, execution, and post‐processing, which can become inefficient and difficult to reproduce when multiple scenarios are analysed, limiting accessibility and broader uptake. Although high‐quality data are essential for research on and conservation of subterranean spiders, such information remains scarce, especially regarding distribution patterns. We asked whether the Canada lynx ( Lynx canadensis ) and the bobcat ( Lynx rufus ) differ in the internal structure of their occupied climatic niches and whether any difference translates into contrasting mid-century projections across North America. We calibrated ensemble species distribution models on 6,721 Canada lynx and 9,030 bobcat records with six climatic predictors per species, compared them in environmental space, and projected suitability to 2041–2060 under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways and three global climate models. The two species occupy divergent observed climatic niches, and the difference is not explained by the climates available to each. item.description:

Developing accurate and cost‐effective methods to detect and predict the spread of invasive species remains an ongoing challenge. Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used to predict invasion under current and future climates and inform management strategies. However, occurrence datasets are often spatially and temporally biased due to unstructured and opportunistic data collection. Remote sensing of individual species over broad spatial and temporal scales has become increasingly feasible with the accumulation of satellite images and the development of convolutional neural networks. In this study, we used 21 years of archival Landsat satellite imagery (2000–2020) to train a land use/land cover (LULC) classification algorithm using a temporal convolutional neural network to predict occurrence of the invasive species, leafy spurge ( Euphorbia virgata ), across Minnesota. Accelerating environmental change in the Antarctic and Southern Ocean (ASO) necessitates robust extinction risk assessments to inform conservation priorities. Nevertheless, no systematic, region-wide baseline of extinction risk currently exists for tracking ASO biodiversity responses to ongoing change, a significant barrier to global biodiversity monitoring. Here, we conducted the first ASO-wide synthesis of current extinction risk knowledge for plants, animals and Fungi. This included examining biases in current assessments, the distribution of Threatened species and their associated threats. Using a data-inclusive workflow, we compiled 8908 assessments representing 4970 species, more than doubling the number of ASO species assessed compared with any single source. item.description:
相关度 69.5 · 关键词匹配：habitat suitability、habitat suitability model、spatial scale

Habitat suitability models (HSMs) use landscape metrics to describe patterns in species distributions, quantify the success of habitat restoration, and model species responses to change. Within a particular level of organization, the spatial scale of effect at which habitat is integrated and incorporated into HSMs can influence model performance. However, scale optimization can be time consuming and requires high-quality data across spatial scales. As such, it is not widely applied in suitability models and is particularly rare in marine studies. In coastal and marine landscapes, or seascapes, rapidly changing seascape metrics and environmental contexts can disrupt known species-seascape relationships and complicate evaluations of habitat quality. item.title: Measuring the edges of species' geographic ranges
item.description:
相关度 79.9 · 关键词匹配：range shift、climatic niche、climate change

The fundamental unit of spatial ecology is a species range: the geographical area that it occupies. Species ranges are delineated by range edges (also known as boundaries or limits). Why range edges occur where they do and not elsewhere, and what makes them move, has been an active area of research since the 19th century. In the present day, range edge dynamics are an important metric of biodiversity's response to climate change, as species shift toward the poles to track their climatic niches. Yet there are many methods for measuring range edges and quantifying their displacement. Here I describe common methods for describing range edge positions and apply them to example data for a bird species and a fish species, using some of the most popular datasets in climate biogeography: the Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count and a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration bottom trawl…

To address this gap, the California Insect Barcoding Initiative is developing a publicly accessible, statewide DNA‐barcode reference library for California insects to support scalable surveys, establish baseline biodiversity measurements, and generate potential distribution maps that inform conservation planning. Specimens are collected with a hybrid strategy that combines standardized Malaise trapping, to enable replicable sampling, and opportunistic collecting, to maximize taxonomic coverage. Here, we establish an integrated, production‐weighted assessment framework coupling SPEI, SSI, and 12 GGCMI3 crop models to trace how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone deficits and crop losses, explicitly separating affected area, conditional yield loss, and accumulated production loss across rainfed maize, soybean, and wheat. Implementing this consideration for coral reef ecosystems is challenging because data describing condition are patchy and limited. To address this uncertainty, we evaluated whether including ecosystem condition data changed conservation priorities when the objective was to protect reefs and implement Target 3. The shapes of species' density distributions reflect how their performance varies across their range – shaped by environment, biotic interactions, and dispersal. Because these distributions reflect emergent properties of populations, they may reveal deterministic processes underlying species' past and future ranges and range shifts. Yet, distribution shape parameters (DSPs) are rarely considered in this context, leaving their potential largely unexplored. The Brazilian coastline is a mosaic of complex marine habitats, including extensive rocky shores and the largest coral reef formation in the Atlantic. By decomposing beta diversity into nestedness and turnover components, we investigated how benthic assemblages are structured and how species composition changes along the transitional zone between rocky and coral reefs. item.description:
相关度 71.4 · 关键词匹配：invasive species

Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. item.title: The science-policy gap on invasive species management: a review of research capacity, regulations, and data availability for an intergovernmental framework in the gulf cooperation council
item.description:
相关度 80.0 · 关键词匹配：invasive species、alien species、risk assessment

Invasive alien species (IAS) pose major threats to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and agriculture, undermining progress on the Sustainable Development Goals. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with its arid climate, rapid urbanisation, dependence on imports, and ecologically fragile, endemic-rich habitats, is especially vulnerable.
